The town’s smallest museum contained only things people had almost thrown away.

A blue button. A bent spoon. A photograph of a dog whose name nobody remembered.

Its curator, a retired mechanic named Ada, opened the doors each morning at nine. Most days nobody came. She dusted anyway.

Under every object was a small handwritten label.

**HOUSE KEY**  
*Found in a coat pocket eleven years after the house was demolished.*

**SHOPPING LIST**  
*Milk, lemons, bread, something nice.*

**SMOOTH STONE**  
*Carried from a beach by someone who believed they would go back.*

One afternoon a boy arrived with an empty glass jar.

“What was in it?” Ada asked.

“A moth.”

“And where is the moth?”

“I let it out.”

Ada turned the jar in her hands. There were three holes punched through the lid, and a twig lay at the bottom.

“My brother says you won’t take it because it’s just rubbish.”

“Your brother hasn’t seen our spoon.”

She found a place for it beside the photograph of the dog.

The boy watched her write the label.

**JAR**  
*Held a moth overnight. The moth was released in the morning.*

“Does it need my name?” he asked.

“Only if you want.”

He thought about this, then shook his head.

The next Saturday he returned with his brother. They went straight to the jar. Ada stayed at her desk, pretending to mend the stapler.

“See?” the boy said.

His brother leaned closer to read the label. After a while, he put his hands in his pockets.

They looked at the rest of the museum, too.
